en-C2-0.b:
Great speakers use rhetorical devices to persuade and to be remembered.

  • Tricolon (rule of three): Government of the people, by the people, for the people. · Faster, cheaper, better.
  • Anaphora: repeating words at the start: We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds…
  • Antithesis: contrasting ideas in parallel: Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country.
  • Rhetorical question: Do we really want to leave this problem to our children?
  • Chiasmus (reversed structure): Eat to live, don't live to eat.
  • Alliteration: Bigger, bolder, brighter.
  • Understatement (very British): It's a bit chilly (in a snowstorm).
  • Hyperbole: I've told you a million times.
  • Metaphor: Time is money. The economy is a ship in a storm.

Tip for public speaking: combine a rhetorical question + a tricolon + a short pause — it's powerful.
en-C2-0.t:
Les grands orateurs utilisent des procédés rhétoriques pour convaincre et marquer les esprits.

  • Rythme ternaire (règle de trois) : Government of the people, by the people, for the people. · Faster, cheaper, better.
  • Anaphore : répéter des mots en début de phrase : We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds…
  • Antithèse : idées opposées en parallèle : Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country.
  • Question rhétorique : Do we really want to leave this problem to our children?
  • Chiasme (structure inversée) : Eat to live, don't live to eat.
  • Allitération : Bigger, bolder, brighter.
  • Euphémisme ironique / litote (très britannique) : It's a bit chilly (en pleine tempête de neige).
  • Hyperbole : I've told you a million times.
  • Métaphore : Time is money. The economy is a ship in a storm.

Astuce pour parler en public : combine une question rhétorique + un rythme ternaire + une courte pause — c'est puissant.
e: We need courage, we need vision, we need action.
Is this really the future we want?
Not because it is easy, but because it is hard.
It's a bit warm today, isn't it? (during a heatwave)
Fortune favours the brave.
q: "Eat to live, don't live to eat" is a ___
"It's a bit chilly" (in a blizzard) is ___
"I've told you a million times" is ___
Repeating words at the start of sentences = ___
"Do we really want this?" (no answer expected) is a ___
"Not because it is easy, but because it is hard" is ___

en-C2-1.b:
At C2, you can move elements of a sentence for focus, style and flow.

  • Fronting (putting the object or complement first for emphasis): That I can't accept. Strange though it may seem, I agree.
  • Inversion after adverbials of place (literary): Here comes the bus. On the hill stood an old castle.
  • End-weight: put long, heavy information at the end: It surprised everyone that he resigned so suddenly (better than « That he resigned so suddenly surprised everyone »).
  • Extraposition with it: It is essential to plan ahead.
  • Adjective order: opinion – size – age – shape – colour – origin – material – purpose: a lovely little old round red Belgian wooden dining table.
  • Adverb position for nuance: Only I saw him (nobody else) / I only saw him (I didn't talk) / I saw only him (no one else).

Common mistake: wrong adjective order: « a wooden old big table » → a big old wooden table.
en-C2-1.t:
Au niveau C2, on peut déplacer des éléments de la phrase pour l'emphase, le style et la fluidité.

  • Antéposition (le complément en tête pour insister) : That I can't accept. (Ça, je ne peux pas l'accepter) Strange though it may seem, I agree. (Aussi étrange que cela paraisse…)
  • Inversion après un complément de lieu (littéraire) : Here comes the bus. On the hill stood an old castle.
  • Poids en fin de phrase : mettre l'information longue à la fin : It surprised everyone that he resigned so suddenly (mieux que « That he resigned so suddenly surprised everyone »).
  • Extraposition avec it : It is essential to plan ahead.
  • Ordre des adjectifs : opinion – taille – âge – forme – couleur – origine – matière – usage : a lovely little old round red Belgian wooden dining table.
  • Place de l'adverbe pour nuancer : Only I saw him (personne d'autre) / I only saw him (je ne lui ai pas parlé) / I saw only him (je n'ai vu que lui).

Erreur fréquente : mauvais ordre des adjectifs : « a wooden old big table » → a big old wooden table.
e: That I simply cannot accept.
Strange though it may seem, I enjoy the rain.
On the corner stood a small café.
It is vital to keep calm under pressure.
She bought a beautiful old Belgian clock.
q: Fronting for emphasis: "___ I can't accept."
Literary inversion: "On the hill ___ an old castle."
Extraposition: "___ is essential to plan ahead."
That he left so suddenly surprised us.
It surprised us that he left so suddenly.
Surprised us it that he left.

en-C2-2.b:
Idioms and figurative language are what make speech colourful and native. Use them naturally, in the right context.

  • to hit the nail on the head: to be exactly right
  • to bite off more than you can chew: to take on too much
  • the elephant in the room: an obvious problem nobody mentions
  • to cut corners: to do something badly to save time or money
  • to be on the same page: to agree / understand the same thing
  • a blessing in disguise: something bad that turns out good
  • to go the extra mile: to make more effort than expected
  • to play devil's advocate: to argue the opposite to test an idea
  • to get the ball rolling: to start something
  • a double-edged sword: something with both advantages and disadvantages

Tips: learn idioms with an example; check the register (many are informal); don't overuse them — one well-placed idiom is more impressive than five.

Common mistake: changing fixed words: « hit the nail on the top » → hit the nail on the head.
en-C2-2.t:
Les expressions idiomatiques et le langage figuré rendent le discours coloré et natif. Utilise-les naturellement, dans le bon contexte.

  • to hit the nail on the head : mettre le doigt dessus, viser juste
  • to bite off more than you can chew : avoir les yeux plus gros que le ventre
  • the elephant in the room : le problème évident que personne n'ose aborder
  • to cut corners : bâcler pour gagner du temps ou de l'argent
  • to be on the same page : être sur la même longueur d'onde
  • a blessing in disguise : un mal pour un bien
  • to go the extra mile : en faire plus que prévu
  • to play devil's advocate : se faire l'avocat du diable
  • to get the ball rolling : lancer les choses
  • a double-edged sword : une arme à double tranchant

Astuces : apprends chaque expression avec un exemple ; vérifie le registre (beaucoup sont familières) ; n'en abuse pas — une expression bien placée impressionne plus que cinq.

Erreur fréquente : changer les mots figés : « hit the nail on the top » → hit the nail on the head.
e: You've hit the nail on the head.
Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.
Let's get the ball rolling with a quick introduction.
Social media is a double-edged sword.
She always goes the extra mile for her clients.
q: "mettre le doigt dessus" = to hit the nail on the ___
"lancer les choses" = to get the ___ rolling
Something with good and bad sides = ___
"être sur la même longueur d'onde" = to be on the same ___

en-C2-3.b:
British (UK) and American (US) English differ in vocabulary, spelling, grammar and pronunciation. Be consistent in writing.

UKUS
flatapartment
liftelevator
holidayvacation
mobile (phone)cell (phone)
queueline
chips / crispsfries / chips
autumnfall
ground floor / first floorfirst floor / second floor
  • Spelling: colour/color, centre/center, organise/organize, travelled/traveled, programme/program.
  • Grammar: UK Have you got…? / US Do you have…?; UK at the weekend / US on the weekend; UK I've just eaten / US also I just ate; collective nouns: UK the team are / US the team is.
  • Dates: UK 5/3 = 5 March; US 5/3 = May 3.

In Belgium and the EU, British English is usually the standard in schools and institutions.
en-C2-3.t:
L'anglais britannique (UK) et américain (US) diffèrent par le vocabulaire, l'orthographe, la grammaire et la prononciation. À l'écrit, reste cohérent.

UKUS
flatapartment (appartement)
liftelevator (ascenseur)
holidayvacation (vacances)
mobile (phone)cell (phone)
queueline (file d'attente)
chips / crispsfries / chips (frites / chips)
autumnfall (automne)
ground floor / first floorfirst floor / second floor (rez-de-chaussée / 1er étage)
  • Orthographe : colour/color, centre/center, organise/organize, travelled/traveled, programme/program.
  • Grammaire : UK Have you got…? / US Do you have…? ; UK at the weekend / US on the weekend ; UK I've just eaten / US aussi I just ate ; noms collectifs : UK the team are / US the team is.
  • Dates : UK 5/3 = 5 mars ; US 5/3 = 3 mai.

En Belgique et dans l'UE, l'anglais britannique est généralement la norme à l'école et dans les institutions.
e: We live in a flat on the third floor.
I'm going on holiday in August.
